The Book

The fire department
carries guns.

Most New Yorkers have no idea. Fire marshals are sworn New York State police officers who arrive after the smoke clears — armed, badged, and responsible for one thing: determining how a fire started, where it originated, and who is going to answer for it. Guns and Hoses takes you from an all-hands job "off the deck" to a felony arson arrest, in the voice of the man who worked it.

Selected Case Files

Real jobs. Real arrests.

Every chapter is built on a documented investigation — interviews, scene examination, origin and cause, and the arrest that followed.

CASE STUDY 01 · QUEENS

Now Do I Have
Your Attention?

May 5, 2019. Three hours into a night tour covering the Bronx, Queens and Upper Manhattan with two marshals. Then SPUDS calls: a child, chained inside a car, set on fire in Springfield Gardens. A 10-45-1 comes over the Queens frequency — and one under.

Priority Response · Fatal Fire
CASE STUDY 02–04 · THE BRONX

My First
Three Arrests

A rookie marshal out of Citywide North at Fort Totten, learning the job the only way it can be learned. A college dormitory fire, two suspects named Cassandra and Jill, a 50 Precinct squad room, and Arson in the Second Degree — a Class B felony.

Arson 2° · Class B Felony
FIELD CRAFT · CITYWIDE

The Art of the
Fire Investigation

How a scene is actually worked: securing access, reading burn patterns, interviewing members and civilians, and documenting findings that must survive criminal trial and civil litigation. The rule never changes — uncover and report the truth.

Origin & Cause · Testimony
From the Manuscript
"How reliable
is this information?"

The call that ends a quiet tour never sounds dramatic. It sounds like a phone ringing in a pizza shop in Flushing while you wait on a meatball parm — and then everything changes, lights and sirens, all the way to Baisley Pond Park.

Read the full chapter free
SPUDS: "Hey boss, what's up? It's Paul from SPUDS."
ME: "What's goin' on, Paul?"
SPUDS: "I just got this notification from FD dispatch that a child was chained into a car and set on fire."
ME: "How reliable is this information?"
SPUDS: "I think it's pretty reliable. Units are still on scene and PD is reporting one under."
ME: "10-4, Paul. Tell the IC that we're responding forthwith."
Inside the Book

What you'll walk
away knowing.

01

Two Jobs, One Person

Firefighter one day, sworn investigator the next. The identity shift from riding a rig with near-zero legal liability to signing findings that put people in handcuffs.

02

How You Become a Marshal

Firefighter first, then seniority, then the promotional exam and fourteen weeks at the Fire Marshal Academy — and why almost nobody joins the FDNY planning on it.

03

Reading the Radio

All-hands, 10-45-1, priority response, jobs "off the deck." Fifty-seven code signals that decide whether a fire becomes a criminal investigation.

04

The Human Cost

Catatonic faces behind crime scene tape. What the job leaves in the people who work it — and the discipline it takes to keep working it anyway.

The Author

Peter
Bradley

Peter Bradley served as an FDNY firefighter, a lieutenant with Ladder 8 in Tribeca, and a Supervising Fire Marshal with the Bureau of Fire Investigation — the busiest fire investigative agency in the country, and most probably the world. Promoted to fire marshal in 2009, he returned to BFI as a supervisor in 2019, running night tours that covered the Bronx, Queens and Manhattan north of 110th Street.

  • FDNY Firefighter · Ladder 31, South Bronx
  • Lieutenant · Ladder 8, Tribeca
  • Supervising Fire Marshal · Squad 53, Citywide North
  • New York State Fire Investigator & Police Officer
"If they gave us the second 'L', the job would be easy."

— FM Bob Cristadoro, BFI mentor
